title: Chapter 6 — Personal Brand and Communication
intro: How you present, speak, write, and follow up — the layer that carries every sale.

sections.title: You Are the Brand
sections.content:
Customers do not buy from stores. They buy from people. When someone refers you, they do not say 'go to that appliance store on Main Street.' They say 'ask for TJ — he is the best.'

Your personal brand is the sum of every interaction. How you answer the phone. How fast you reply to texts. How you handle a complaint. Whether you remember their name. Whether you follow through on what you promised. Whether your emails are professional or sloppy.

Every touchpoint either builds your brand or damages it. There is no neutral interaction.

sections.title: Communication That Builds Trust
sections.content:
Professional communication is not about being formal. It is about being clear, reliable, and human.

Say 'I will' not 'I will try.' Say 'Here is what I can do' not 'That is our policy.' Say 'I understand' without adding 'but.' Use their name — twice in a conversation is perfect. More than that gets creepy. Less than that is forgettable.

Response time is a promise. Phone calls returned within an hour. Emails within four hours during business hours. Texts within 30 minutes. Every unanswered message is a customer wondering if you care.

sections.title: Social Media as a Sales Tool
sections.content:
Your personal social media is a sales tool. Not the store page — YOUR page. Customers Google you. They check your Instagram. They look you up on LinkedIn. What they find either builds trust or loses the sale before you meet them.

Post beautiful kitchens you helped design. Film 30-second product demos — open the fridge, pull the dishwasher racks, light the burners. Share customer wins with permission. Post educational content that positions you as an expert.

Do not post pricing — that is a MAP violation. Do not bash competitors. Do not post complaints about work. Do not post political opinions on your professional page.

Consistency beats virality. Three to five posts per week. After six months, you will start getting DMs from people who found you online. That is a warm lead that cost you nothing except consistency.

sections.title: Written Communication Standards
sections.content:
Every email you send is a permanent record of your professionalism. One typo in a $10,000 quote makes you look careless. A sloppy follow-up email makes the customer wonder if your attention to detail extends to their order.

Keep emails short. Lead with the action item. Use their name. End with a clear next step. Proofread everything — especially model numbers and prices, because those errors cost real money.

Text messages should feel like they are from a friend who happens to sell appliances. Keep them under three sentences. No ALL CAPS. One exclamation mark maximum. Always identify yourself in the first text.

The golden rule of written communication: every message should either answer a question, provide information, or give them a reason to respond. If it does none of those, do not send it.
